sections.name: Red Teaming: Adversary Simulation
sections.explanation_simple: Red teaming is the most advanced form of security testing. Unlike a regular penetration test where you test specific vulnerabilities, a red team exercise simulates a real, sophisticated attacker. The red team has a goal (access a specific server, steal specific data) and uses any means necessary - phishing, physical intrusion, social engineering, zero-day exploits, persistence, and lateral movement. Red team operations typically last weeks or months and test the full detection and response capabilities of the blue team. It's like a fire drill for your security team, except the 'fire' is a team of expert hackers trying to break in.
key_concepts: Adversary Emulation: Mimicking a specific threat actor's TTPs (MITRE ATT&CK)
C2 (Command & Control): Infrastructure that the red team uses to control compromised systems
Cobalt Strike: Most popular red team framework (commercial, $3,500/year)
Sliver: Open-source C2 framework (free, becoming very popular)
Mythic: Another open-source C2 framework with many agents
Phishing: Sending convincing emails to trick users into clicking malicious links
Spear Phishing: Targeted phishing at specific individuals (researched and customized)
SMTP Relay: Setting up email servers for phishing (or using services like SendGrid)
Payload Delivery: Getting your initial foothold (macro, ISO, LNK, HTML smuggling)
Initial Access: The first compromise (usually phishing or exposed service)
Lateral Movement: Moving from the first compromised machine to other systems
Persistence: Maintaining access even after reboots (scheduled tasks, services, WMI)
Privilege Escalation: Getting from limited user to admin/system
Domain Dominance: Compromising the Domain Controller (game over for Active Directory)
Data Exfiltration: Getting the target data out without being detected
OpSec: Operational Security - not getting caught (covering tracks, living off the land)
Living Off the Land: Using built-in OS tools (PowerShell, WMI, certutil) instead of dropping malware
TTPs: Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (how a specific attacker operates)

sections.name: Blue Teaming: Detection & Incident Response
sections.explanation_simple: Blue teaming is the defensive side of cybersecurity. While red teams simulate attackers, blue teams detect and stop them. A blue team's job includes: monitoring security alerts, analyzing suspicious activity, containing threats, and improving defenses. The most important tools are SIEM (Security Information and Event Management - collects and analyzes logs from everywhere), EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response - monitors individual computers for malicious activity), and SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response - automates incident response). The key skill is being able to tell the difference between a real attack and a false alarm.
key_concepts: SIEM: Centralized log collection and analysis (Splunk, Elastic Security, Wazuh, Sentinel)
EDR: Endpoint monitoring (CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Defender for Endpoint)
XDR: Extended Detection and Response - SIEM + EDR + network + cloud
SOAR: Automated incident response playbooks
Log Analysis: Finding attacks in mountains of log data
Correlation: Connecting related events across different systems
Alert Triage: Quickly determining if an alert is real or false positive
Incident Response (IR): Structured process for handling security incidents
Phases of IR: Preparation -> Detection -> Containment -> Eradication -> Recovery -> Lessons Learned
Threat Hunting: Proactively searching for threats that evaded automated detection
IOC (Indicator of Compromise): Evidence of a breach (IP, hash, domain, registry key)
IOA (Indicator of Attack): Behavior patterns indicating an attack in progress
Sigma Rules: Generic detection rules that can be converted to any SIEM format
Playbook: Step-by-step guide for handling specific incident types (ransomware, phishing, data breach)
Ransomware: The most critical incident type - every blue team needs a playbook for this

code_examples.title: Incident Response Playbook: Ransomware
code_examples.code:
# ===== RANSOMWARE INCIDENT RESPONSE PLAYBOOK =====

"""
SEVERITY: CRITICAL - Activate immediately

=== STEP 1: DECLARE INCIDENT ===
- Notify: SOC Manager, On-Call Incident Commander, Legal
- Start IR log (timeline of every action taken)
- Preserve all evidence before taking action

=== STEP 2: CONTAINMENT (Stop the spread) ===
[ ] Isolate affected systems from network
    - Pull network cable / disable Wi-Fi
    - Do NOT shut down (loses evidence)
[ ] Disable Active Directory account if user account compromised
[ ] Block ransomware C2 IPs on firewall
[ ] Disable SMB if propagation is active
[ ] Power off unaffected systems in same segment

=== STEP 3: ERADICATION (Remove the threat) ===
[ ] Identify patient zero (how did it get in?)
[ ] Scan all systems for IOCs
[ ] Remove persistence mechanisms
[ ] Reset compromised credentials
[ ] Patch vulnerability used for initial access

=== STEP 4: RECOVERY (Restore operations) ===
[ ] Restore from clean backups
    - Verify backup integrity before restoring
    - Scan restored files before bringing online
[ ] Wipe and reimage affected systems
[ ] Bring systems back in priority order

=== STEP 5: COMMUNICATION ===
[ ] Internal: Leadership, Legal, PR, affected teams
[ ] External: Law enforcement (if required by policy)
[ ] Regulatory: If PII/PHI involved (GDPR: 72 hours)
[ ] Public: If customer data affected (coordinated with PR)

=== STEP 6: POST-MORTEM ===
[ ] Root cause analysis (how did this happen?)
[ ] Identify gaps in defenses
[ ] Implement improvements
[ ] Update playbook

--- TECHNICAL TRIAGE COMMANDS ---
"""

# PowerShell: Quick triage of a potentially infected system

Write-Host "=== RANSOMWARE TRIAGE ===" -ForegroundColor Red

# 1. Check for file encryption in progress
Write-Host "[1] Checking for mass file operations..."
# Look for processes with high file write activity
Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.Responding -eq $true } | Sort-Object -Property WorkingSet -Descending | Select-Object -First 10

# 2. Check for known ransomware extensions
$ransom_extensions = @('.encrypted','.locked','.crypt','.cryptolocker','.locky','.wncry','.wcry')
foreach ($ext in $ransom_extensions) {
    $count = (Get-ChildItem -Path C:\ -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue -Filter "*$ext" | Measure-Object).Count
    if ($count -gt 0) {
        Write-Host "[!] Found $count files with $ext extension" -ForegroundColor Red
    }
}

# 3. Check for ransom notes
$ransom_notes = @('README','DECRYPT','HELP_DECRYPT','HOW_TO_DECRYPT','RESTORE_FILES')
foreach ($note in $ransom_notes) {
    $found = Get-ChildItem -Path C:\ -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue -Include "$note*" | Select-Object -First 1
    if ($found) {
        Write-Host "[!] Ransom note found: $($found.FullName)" -ForegroundColor Red
        $content = Get-Content $found.FullName -First 5 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
        Write-Host "Content: $content"
    }
}

# 4. Check volume shadow copies (ransomware deletes them)
$vss = Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_ShadowCopy -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Write-Host "[i] Volume Shadow Copies: $($vss.Count) available"
if ($vss.Count -eq 0) { Write-Host "[!] Shadow copies deleted (ransomware signature)" -ForegroundColor Red }

# 5. Check network connections
Write-Host "[5] Checking suspicious outbound connections..."
$suspiciousPorts = @(4444, 1337, 8080, 8888, 9999)
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Established | Where-Object { $_.RemotePort -in $suspiciousPorts } | Format-Table

# 6. Check scheduled tasks (ransomware often adds persistence)
Write-Host "[6] Checking new scheduled tasks..."
$recentlyModified = (Get-Date).AddHours(-24)
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.Date -gt $recentlyModified -and $_.TaskPath -notlike '*Microsoft*' } | Format-Table TaskName, TaskPath

# 7. Get process tree to find parent processes
Write-Host "[7] Process tree for suspicious processes..."
Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Where-Object { $_.Name -match '(powershell|cmd|wscript|cscript|rundll32)' } |
    Select-Object ProcessId, Name, CommandLine, @{N='ParentPID';E={$_.ParentProcessId}}

code_examples.title: SIEM Detection Rule (Splunk) & Sigma
code_examples.code:
# ===== SPLUNK DETECTION SEARCHES =====

"""
1. DETECT POWERSHELL ENCODED COMMAND
"""
index=windows EventCode=4104 ScriptBlockText=*EncodedCommand*
| stats count by ComputerName, UserId
| where count > 3

"""
2. DETECT PASS-THE-HASH (NTLM anomaly)"""
index=windows EventCode=4624 LogonType=3 (network)
 NOT (WorkstationName=*$)
| stats count by AccountName, WorkstationName, IpAddress
| where count > 50

"""
3. DETECT RANSOMWARE: Mass file deletions"""
index=windows EventCode=4656 (file accessed)
 ObjectName=*.{docx,xlsx,pptx,pdf,jpg,png}
| bucket _time span=5m
| stats dc(ObjectName) as unique_files by ComputerName, _time
| where unique_files > 100

"""
4. DETECT LATERAL MOVEMENT (SMB)"""
index=windows EventCode=4624 LogonType=3
 AccountName!={SYSTEM, LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE}
| stats values(SourceIP) as source_ips by ComputerName, AccountName
| where mvcount(source_ips) > 1

# ===== SIGMA RULE (convertible to ANY SIEM) =====
title: PowerShell Download From Suspicious Domain
id: xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx
status: experimental
description: Detects PowerShell downloading files from suspicious domains
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
author: SOC Team
date: 2024/01/01
tags:
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.defense_evasion
    - attack.t1140
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - 'DownloadString('
            - 'DownloadFile('
            - 'Invoke-WebRequest'
            - 'wget'
            - 'curl'
            - 'Start-BitsTransfer'
    filter:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'github.com'
            - 'microsoft.com'
            - 'powershellgallery.com'
    condition: selection and not filter
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative scripts downloading tools from approved sources
level: medium

# Convert Sigma to Splunk:
# sigma convert -t splunk sigma_rule.yml

# Convert Sigma to Elasticsearch/KQL:
# sigma convert -t es-qs sigma_rule.yml

# Convert Sigma to Microsoft Sentinel:
# sigma convert -t sentinel sigma_rule.yml

sections.name: Digital Forensics & Incident Response (DFIR)
sections.explanation_simple: Digital forensics is the investigation of computer systems to find evidence of a crime or security incident. It follows strict procedures to ensure evidence is admissible in court (chain of custody, write blockers, cryptographic hashing). The main areas are disk forensics (analyzing hard drives for deleted files, artifacts, and timeline reconstruction), memory forensics (analyzing RAM for running processes, injected code, encryption keys), and network forensics (analyzing packet captures for evidence of communication with attackers). Volatility is the most important memory forensics tool, and Autopsy/Sleuth Kit are the standards for disk forensics.
key_concepts: Chain of Custody: Documentation of who handled evidence and when (critical for legal admissibility)
Write Blocker: Hardware device that prevents any writes to a forensic drive (read-only access)
Forensic Image: Bit-for-bit copy of a drive (dd, E01, AFF formats)
Hashing: MD5/SHA256 of the original evidence to prove it wasn't modified
File Carving: Recovering deleted files by finding file headers in unallocated space
Master File Table (MFT): NTFS index of every file on the volume (goldmine of forensic data)
USN Journal: NTFS change journal (every file modification - critical for timeline)
Prefetch: Windows files that track program execution (shows what ran and when)
ShimCache/AmCache: Windows artifacts showing program execution (undocumented, very useful)
Jump Lists: Windows recent files lists (shows what files the user opened)
Recycle Bin: Shows deleted files (even after emptying, metadata remains)
Registry Analysis: NTUSER.DAT, SAM, SYSTEM, SOFTWARE hives (user activity, accounts, config)
Memory Acquisition: Capturing RAM contents (dumpit.exe, winpmem, LiME for Linux)
Volatility: Memory analysis framework (most important forensic tool)
Timeline Analysis: Reconstructing the sequence of events (critical for understanding incidents)
Browser Forensics: History, bookmarks, cookies, saved passwords (major evidence source)
Email Forensics: Headers analysis, deleted emails, mailbox artifacts
Mobile Forensics: Physical vs logical acquisition, app data extraction

code_examples.title: Memory Forensics with Volatility 3
code_examples.code:
# ===== VOLATILITY 3 MEMORY ANALYSIS =====
# Volatility is the industry standard for memory forensics
# Install: pip install volatility3

"""
MEMORY ACQUISITION (before analysis):

Windows:
  dumpit.exe -o memory.dmp (DumpIt from Comae)
  winpmem.exe -o memory.raw (WinPMEM from Velocidex)

Linux:
  sudo ./linpmem -o memory.raw
  sudo insmod lime.ko "path=memory.dump format=lime"

macOS:
  sudo ./macpmem -o memory.raw
"""

# ===== VOLATILITY 3 COMMANDS =====

# 1. Get system information
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.info
# Output: OS version, kernel base, number of CPUs, etc.

# 2. List running processes
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.pslist
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.psscan  # Uses pool scanning (finds hidden processes!)

# 3. Show process tree (parent-child relationships)
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.pstree

# 4. List network connections
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.netscan
# Shows: connections, listening ports, associated processes

# 5. Extract command line arguments
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.cmdline.CmdLine
# Critical: shows ALL command lines of running processes

# 6. Dump a specific process (for malware analysis)
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.dumpfiles.DumpFiles --pid 1234

# 7. Extract process environment variables
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.envars.Envars --pid 1234

# 8. Scan for injected code (MALICIOUS!)
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.malfind.Malfind
# Shows memory pages that are: executable, writable, but not a known DLL
# This is how you find process injection

# 9. Scan for handles (files, registry keys, etc. that a process has open)
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.handles.Handles --pid 1234

# 10. Extract clipboard contents
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.clipboard

# 11. Extract registry hives
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.registry.hivescan
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.registry.printkey -K "HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Services"

# 12. Scan for Windows User Accounts
python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.hashdump.Hashdump
# Dumps NTLM hashes (like Mimikatz from memory)

# ===== ANALYZING SUSPICIOUS PROCESS =====
# Full workflow for investigating PID 4321:

vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.malfind.Malfind --pid 4321  # Check for injection
vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.cmdline.CmdLine --pid 4321  # Check command line
vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.handles.Handles --pid 4321  # Check handles
vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.dlllist --pid 4321          # List loaded DLLs
vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.netscan --pid 4321          # Network connections
vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.dumpfiles --pid 4321        # Dump for further analysis

# ===== TIMELINE CREATION =====
# Create a timeline of all events from memory
vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.timeliner.Timeliner > timeline.csv
# Then analyze in Timeline Explorer (open source tool) or Excel

code_examples.title: Disk Forensics & Autopsy Workflow
code_examples.code:
# ===== AUTOPSY/SLEUTH KIT DISK FORENSICS =====

"""
DISK ACQUISITION:

  Physical acquisition (dd):
    dd if=/dev/sda of=evidence.dd bs=4096 conv=noerror,sync status=progress

  Forensic image with metadata (ewfacquire):
    ewfacquire /dev/sda evidence.E01
    - Compresses the image
    - Stores metadata (case number, examiner, hash)
    - Splits into manageable chunks

  Windows (FTK Imager):
    File -> Create Disk Image
    - Evidence can be live or from write-blocked drive

KEY FORENSIC ARTIFACTS TO CHECK:
"""

# ===== WINDOWS FORENSIC ARTIFACTS =====
$artifacts = @"

1. PREFETCH FILES
   Location: C:\Windows\Prefetch\*.pf
   What: Shows what programs ran, when, and how many times
   Tool: PECmd.exe (Eric Zimmerman)

2. JUMP LISTS
   Location: C:\Users\%user%\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Recent\*
   What: Shows recently opened files per application
   Tool: JLECmd.exe

3. SHIMCACHE
   Location: Registry (SYSTEM hive)
   What: Shows program execution (even if deleted!)
   Tool: AppCompatCacheParser.exe (Eric Zimmerman)

4. RECYCLE BIN
   Location: C:\$Recycle.Bin\*
   What: Shows deleted files with original paths
   Tool: RBCmd.exe

5. REGISTRY
   NTUSER.DAT: User configuration, MRU lists, typed URLs
   SAM: Local user account hashes
   SYSTEM: System configuration, mounted devices, services
   SOFTWARE: Installed programs, Windows settings

6. EVENT LOGS
   Location: C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\*.evtx
   Security: Logons, logoffs, privilege use, policy changes
   System: Service start/stop, driver loads, errors
   PowerShell: Script execution (if enabled)

7. USN JOURNAL
   Location: C:\$Extend\$UsnJrnl:$J
   What: Every file change ever (name, timestamp, reason)
   Critical for tracking malware file creation!

8. BROWSER ARTIFACTS
   Chrome: C:\Users\%user%\AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\
     - History, Downloads, Login Data (passwords), Cookies
   Firefox: C:\Users\%user%\AppData\Roaming\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*
   Edge: Similar to Chrome (Chromium-based)

"@

Write-Host $artifacts

# ===== TIMELINE ANALYSIS POWERSHELL =====
$timelineQuery = @"
"""
Use MFTEcmd.exe (MFT parser) to create a timeline:
  MFTEcmd.exe -f C:\$MFT --de 5 --csv timeline.csv

This produces a CSV with EVERY file operation:
  - File creation time
  - File modification time
  - MFT modification time
  - Access time
  - File size
  - Parent directory
  - File name

In Excel/SQL:
  1. Sort by creation time (oldest first)
  2. Look at files created around the incident time
  3. Look for: EXE, DLL, PS1, VBS, JS, BAT files
  4. Check if they were created by unusual processes
  5. Trace back to the source process
"""

# ===== KEY FORENSIC QUESTIONS =====
"""
For every investigation, answer:

1. THREAT IDENTIFICATION
   - What is the malware/attack?
   - What is the indicator of compromise (IOC)?

2. INFECTION VECTOR
   - How did it enter? (Phishing? Drive-by? USB?)
   - What file/download/email was the initial vector?

3. SCOPE
   - Which systems are affected?
   - What data was accessed/exfiltrated?

4. TIMELINE
   - When did the initial compromise happen?
   - When did lateral movement occur?
   - When was data exfiltrated?

5. ROOT CAUSE
   - What vulnerability was exploited?
   - What misconfiguration allowed spread?
   - What security control was missing?
"""

sections.name: Wireless Security Auditing
sections.explanation_simple: Wireless security is about securing Wi-Fi networks and other wireless communications (Bluetooth, RFID, NFC, Zigbee). Wi-Fi is inherently less secure than wired because the signal travels through the air - anyone within range can attempt to connect or eavesdrop. Modern WPA3 is very secure, but many networks still use WPA2 (which can be cracked with enough time) or worse, WEP (which can be cracked in seconds). Wireless auditing involves checking network configurations, identifying weak encryption, detecting rogue access points, and testing for vulnerabilities in the wireless infrastructure.
key_concepts: SSID: Network name (don't broadcast? Not real security - easily found)
BSSID: MAC address of the access point
WEP: Oldest security protocol (COMPLETELY broken - can crack in seconds)
WPA: Transitional protocol (TKIP encryption - also broken)
WPA2: Current standard (AES/CCMP encryption - can crack with dictionary attack on weak passwords)
WPA3: Newest standard (SAE handshake - resistant to dictionary attacks, much more secure)
PMKID: Key derived from password that can be used for cracking (even without clients!)
4-Way Handshake: The cryptographic exchange between client and AP (contains the password hash)
Rogue AP: Fake access point that looks legitimate (evil twin attack)
Deauthentication Attack: Disconnecting a client from their AP (forces reconnection - captures handshake)
Krack Attack: Vulnerability in WPA2's 4-way handshake (allows reinstallation of encryption key)
WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup): PIN-based setup - Bruteforce-able in hours
Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE): Short-range wireless (used by IoT devices, often insecure)
Bluetooth Hacking: BlueBorne, BlueSmack, Bluetooth Impersonation Attacks (BIAS)
SDR (Software Defined Radio): Using a radio receiver to analyze any wireless communication
RFID/NFC Hacking: Cloning access cards, payment card information

code_examples.title: Wi-Fi Security Audit with aircrack-ng
code_examples.code:
# ===== WIFI SECURITY AUDIT USING AIRCRACK-NG =====
# Educational: For auditing your OWN network security

"""
PREREQUISITES:
  - Linux (Kali/Parrot recommended)
  - Wireless card that supports monitor mode (Alfa AWUS036ACH is standard)
  - aircrack-ng suite

STEP 1: Put wireless card in monitor mode
"""
# Check wireless interfaces
# airmon-ng

# Kill interfering processes
# airmon-ng check kill

# Enable monitor mode on wlan0
# airmon-ng start wlan0
# Now your interface is wlan0mon

"""
STEP 2: Scan for networks
"""
# airodump-ng wlan0mon

# This shows:
# BSSID - MAC of access point
# PWR - Signal strength
# CH - Channel
# ENC - Encryption (WEP, WPA, WPA2, WPA3)
# ESSID - Network name
# STATION - Connected clients

"""
STEP 3: Capture the 4-way handshake
"""
# Focus on a specific target:
# airodump-ng -c 6 --bssid AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -w capture wlan0mon

# Wait for a client to connect, OR force a reconnect:
# aireplay-ng -0 2 -a AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF wlan0mon
# -0 = deauthentication attack
# 2 = send 2 deauth packets (usually enough)
# -a = target AP

"""
STEP 4: Crack the password
"""
# Using a wordlist:
# aircrack-ng -w /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt capture-01.cap

# Using hashcat (GPU accelerated - MUCH faster):
# Convert cap to hashcat format:
# cap2hccapx capture-01.cap capture.hccapx
# hashcat -m 22000 -a 0 capture.hccapx rockyou.txt

# Using mask attack (try all 8-digit numeric):
# hashcat -m 22000 -a 3 capture.hccapx ?d?d?d?d?d?d?d?d

"""
WPA3 NOTE: WPA3 uses SAE handshake which is resistant
to dictionary attacks. The only way to crack WPA3 is
to attack weak passwords through the SAE handshake,
which is MUCH slower than WPA2 cracking.
"""

# ===== WPS PIN ATTACK =====
# Many routers have WPS enabled (even if you can't find the button)
# WPS PIN is 8 digits, but the last digit is a checksum
# And it's validated in two halves - so only 7 digits to crack!
# 10^4 (first half) + 10^3 (second half) = 11,000 attempts max

# Use reaver or bully:
# reaver -i wlan0mon -b AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -vv
# bully -i wlan0mon -b AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF

# ===== ROGUE AP DETECTION =====
# Wireshark filter to find fake access points:
wlan.fc.type_subtype == 8  # Beacon frames

# Look for:
# 1. APs with same SSID but different BSSID (evil twin)
# 2. APs not on your authorized list
# 3. APs with unusually strong signal (attacker nearby)
# 4. APs with open encryption (no password)

# ===== BLUETOOTH AUDIT TOOLS =====
# Scan for Bluetooth devices:
# hcitool scan
# bleah -b (BLE device scan)
# bluez-test-discovery

# Classic Bluetooth attacks:
# bluetoothctl
# l2ping -f <MAC>  (DoS - flood with pings)
# btscanner

# BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) analysis:
# gatttool -b <MAC> -I  # Interact with BLE devices
# Bettercap with BLE module:
# sudo bettercap -eval "ble.enum LEAA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF"

sections.learning_path: Wireless fundamentals (802.11 standards) -> Monitor mode setup -> WEP cracking -> WPA2 handshake capture -> Password cracking (dictionary, mask, rule-based) -> PMKID attack -> WPS PIN attack -> Evil twin/Rogue AP -> Bluetooth security -> BLE analysis -> RFID/NFC cloning -> SDR basics -> Wireless IDS deployment -> Rogue AP detection
